But after the Balogun affair, a fired-up Belgium quashed those hopes last month with a crushing 4-1 victory.

title: UEFA threatens FIFA with legal action over failed plan to sell World Cup stakes
content:
European football body UEFA has threatened FIFA with legal action over Gianni Infantino's failed plan to sell a stake in future World Cup profits to private investors, and said any potential evidence should not be destroyed.
Infantino's secretive proposal to raise $4.2 billion from investors including the New York investment firm of Joshua Kushner was dropped early on Saturday (August 1, 2026), days after the revelation in media reports provoked a global furor.
UEFA led the backlash and on Thursday (July 30) its 55 member federations met to agree boycotting all FIFA events and competitions while the proposal was active.
Now lawyers for UEFA have informed FIFA that the European body is “actively considering legal action, arbitration, and/or regulatory complaints ... arising out of and in connection with the FFE (FIFA Forward Enterprise) plan proposed by FIFA and all related matters.”
The letter dated Friday from the legal firm Dechert in New York was seen on Monday (August 3) by The Associated Press.
The letter named 18 FIFA executives who it said should retain data, documents and electronic messages as potential evidence. They include Infantino, Zurich-based chief finance officer Thomas Peyer and Arsène Wenger, the coaching great who is FIFA's head of global soccer development.
“UEFA puts you on formal notice that any destruction, deletion, alteration, concealment, or loss of relevant materials following receipt of this notice — or following any earlier date on which you were, or reasonably should have been, aware that proceedings were anticipated — may constitute spoliation of evidence,” the letter said.
Europe seeks rival candidate to lead FIFA The Swedish soccer federation confirmed on Monday (August 3) that UEFA is actively looking "to come up with an alternative candidate” as FIFA president. The next election is scheduled in March.
On Saturday (August 1), UEFA signalled it wants to end Infantino's decade-long presidency, saying he had lost the confidence of world soccer and that “no option should be off the table.”
Hours earlier, Infantino had withdrawn the divisive proposal that offered FIFA's 211 member federations one-off payments of $20 million each with a mid-September deadline to accept.
off valued by FIFA at $20 billion would have taken control of the soccer body's money-making commercial and tournament operations through at least 2038. It promised to more than double development money over that time for the 211 members who already effectively own the Zurich-based not-for-profit governing body.
It was the project of just one man, FIFA's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said in a stinging statement Friday to the AP which said staff felt deceived by their boss Infantino.
Legal proceedings are “reasonably anticipated,” UEFA's lawyer Andrew J. Levander wrote, citing the belief of soccer stakeholders that the plan was “fundamentally incompatible with the proper governance of football.” Opposition to InfantinoUEFA has been most outspoken against its former employee Infantino while the Asian Football Confederation and CONCACAF, the North and Central American and Caribbean soccer body, also have made strong statements to oppose Infantino's plan.
Infantino has most support from his traditional base in Africa, while South America's CONMEBOL is relying on him to expand the 2030 World Cup to 64 teams from 48. That would give more hosting games to Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay, the home country of CONMEBOL president Alejandro Dominguez.
Infantino's path to stabilizing the presidency he has held for 10 1/2 years was unclear on Monday (August 3) which began in New York with a report he was seeking support from the administration of his close ally U.S. President Donald Trump, possibly in a call with Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
“There are no plans for @SecRubio to speak with Infantino and there is no call this morning,” Dylan Johnson, assistant secretary of state for global public affairs, posted on social media.
The private equity plan has provoked a stunning turnaround in fortunes for Infantino since it was revealed last Tuesday (July 28) by The Times of London.
The 56-year-old FIFA leader left New York after the World Cup final two weeks ago seemingly a lock to be re-elected unopposed next March for a fourth and final term in office through 2031.
off operation could have created a commissioner-like role for him beyond 2031 paying much more than his current $6 million annual salary and bonus deal as president.
FIFA briefed at the World Cup that Infantino had got pledged letters of support from about 200 of the 211 member federations.
Those letters are now likely being withdrawn across Europe with the Wales federation the first to announce its reversal.
The candidate deadline is Nov. 18 for an election exactly four months later in Morocco, one of Infantino's strongest allies and a co-host of the 2030 tournament with Spain and Portugal.

title: Dravidian Cricket League-2026 launched in Kuppam
content:
Chancellor L.C. Mallaiah inaugurated the 10-day Dravidian Cricket League-2026 at the Indira Gandhi Open Air Stadium on the campus here on Monday. The Vice-Chancellor also joined the students in a friendly cricket match as part of the league’s inauguration. The league aims to promote sportsmanship and student participation in competitive games.
Addressing the students and faculty, Mr. Mallaiah said that regular participation in sports improves physical fitness, mental well-being, discipline and leadership qualities, while also preparing students for higher-level competitions. Faculty members, non-teaching staff and students attended the inaugural programme.

title: ‘Who approved it?’: HI president Dilip Tirkey seeks answers on jersey switch
content:
What began as a controversy over the Indian hockey team’s switch from its traditional blue jersey to saffron has now snowballed into a governance battle within Hockey India (HI).
In a strongly worded letter to the federation’s director general (DG), Cdr RK Srivastava, HI president Dilip Tirkey has raised serious questions over authority, accountability and transparency in the decision-making process behind the jersey change.
The letter, accessed by TOI, is Tirkey’s response to Srivastava’s July 31 explanation on the approval process. Questioning who authorised the redesign and whether due process was followed, Tirkey has sought answers from the federation’s administrative leadership, deepening the controversy.
Describing the DG’s four-page reply as largely off the point, Tirkey wrote: “...the issue under consideration is not merely the colour or design of a playing jersey. The matter concerns the decision-making process adopted for a change involving one of the most recognisable symbols of Indian hockey, the authority under which such a decision was taken, the consultations undertaken, compliance with Hockey India’s governance framework, and whether appropriate institutional processes were followed.
“Hockey India is a custodian of a legacy. Decisions affecting such symbols must therefore be approached with the highest standards of governance, transparency and accountability.”
Tirkey also questioned why the elected Executive Board was bypassed. Revealing that he learnt about the redesigned jersey only through a WhatsApp group message a few hours before its social media launch on July 27, Tirkey wrote: “The Director General has an important executive and administrative role in managing the affairs of Hockey India and implementing approved decisions. However, administrative responsibility cannot be interpreted as replacing or overriding the authority of the elected governance bodies. Given the importance and national significance of the decision, the Executive Board requires clarification as to why the President and the Executive Board were not consulted before the public announcement.”
The 412-cap India veteran also took exception to a section of the DG’s reply that detailed HI’s high-performance initiatives.
“The Executive Board is fully familiar with the demands of elite sport and high-performance environments. The EB includes several distinguished former international players and Olympians who have personally experienced the demands of preparing for and performing at the highest levels of hockey... and fully recognises that modern sport requires continuous improvement and that every genuine marginal gain must be pursued,” Tirkey wrote.
With the controversy erupting less than three weeks before the FIH Hockey World Cup begins in the Netherlands and Belgium on Aug 15, Tirkey also questioned the timing of the change.
“A decision intended to improve performance must not inadvertently create uncertainty, distraction or disruption at a critical stage of preparation. It is therefore necessary for the Executive Board to understand how the jersey change was assessed within the overall high-performance plan,” he said.
Tirkey has sought a comprehensive reply from the DG, supported by documentary evidence, by 5 pm on Tuesday.
Signing off, he wrote: “Hockey India does not own Indian hockey. We are trustees and custodians of a national sporting legacy”.

title: Glasgow done, all eyes on 'Amdavad 2030': India's campaign offers both promise and warning signs
content:
The Glasgow Commonwealth Games are over. The baton passes to India for the Commonwealth Games in Ahmedabad, dubbed ‘Amdavad 2030’. With the event returning home after 20 years, India will be aiming not only to stage a better Games than Delhi 2010 but also to improve on its best-ever medal haul. At the 2010 Delhi Games, India won a record 101 medals to finish second in the overall standings.
For Indian sport, Glasgow offered a mixed picture. The 39 medals collected this time were fewer than the 61 in Birmingham 2022, 66 in Gold Coast 2018 and 64 in Glasgow 2014. More importantly, those medals came from just six sports. By contrast, India’s medals had come from 17 sports in 2010, 11 in 2014, 15 in 2018 and 13 in 2022.
The explanation lies partly in the programme itself. Glasgow did not include sports where India has traditionally been strong. India has won 135 medals in shooting between 1966 and 2018, excluding the 1970 Edinburgh edition. Wrestling has fetched India 114 medals across 18 editions since 1934. Yet Glasgow had no shooting, wrestling, hockey, badminton, archery or table tennis, which together had contributed 67 medals for India in Delhi 2010.
As India prepares to host in 2030, the focus will be on retaining the positives from Glasgow while also bringing back its strongest disciplines.
Athletics emerged as the biggest winner for India, with medals in the men’s 10,000m and 5,000m long jump, decathlon, high jump, triple jump and para-athletics adding up to 16 medals. What stood out most was the history made by Gulveer Singh, who won silver in the 10,000m and bronze in the 5,000m and Tejaswin Shankar, who claimed decathlon bronze.
Yash Vir Singh also broke new ground by winning a javelin bronze in a field featuring Olympic and world champions, as well as world leaders and record holders. The para-athletes contributed three gold, two silver and one bronze, even as the 4x400m relay team had to settle for sixth place.
“The performance was way better than expected. This has been a good result and it will only improve in the years to come. The result reflects the policies that the Athletics Federation of India (AFI) has adopted in the past few years,” former World Championships bronze medallist and current AFI senior vice-president Anju Bobby George told TOI.
“Now we plan the training programme according to individual athletes’ requirements rather than designing a blanket programme for everyone. Some athletes train in the USA, some in Europe, because that is what best suits their future. The results are definitely going to improve in 2030 and beyond, as we also plan to host the Olympics,” she added.
Boxing also delivered strongly, with seven gold among the 13 medals won. While the level of competition at the Commonwealth Games is not as demanding as at the Asian Games or Olympics, the performances will still provide a valuable confidence boost.
“It is not as if these were the only medals our boxers have won so far. We had world champions, an Olympic medallist and Asian Games and Asian Championships winners at the Glasgow CWG. The field may not have been as strong as the Asiad, but it was not weak either.
A good show at a competition like this gives a boost to the boxers,” 2008 Beijing Olympics bronze medallist Vijender Singh told TOI.
Judokas earn their place in the spotlight
With two historic gold and three medals overall, Indian judokas Asmita Dey, Harsh Singh and Yamini Mourya also deserve special mention. A sport that has often struggled for attention in the past appears to be finding its footing.
If judo can continue on this trajectory, the possibilities are immense. With 15 medal events at the Olympics and proper investment and a cleaner administrative setup, India has genuine medal potential at the world level too.

title: World Cup rights row: Wales withdraw support for Infantino's re-election bid
content:
Wales have become the first home nation to withdraw support for Gianni Infantino's bid to remain FIFA president after his proposal to sell a stake in the commercial rights of the World Cup and other FIFA competitions was abandoned.
The Football Association of Wales (FAW) said it will no longer back Infantino's re-election campaign for the 2027-2031 term, following concerns over the failed investment plan.
FIFA had proposed raising up to $4.2 billion by selling about a 20% stake in a new entity that would manage the commercial rights of competitions including the World Cup. However, the proposal was withdrawn on Friday after facing strong opposition from stakeholders.
With the plan shelved, attention has shifted to the possible impact on Infantino's chances of securing another term as FIFA president.
The proposal had also triggered strong criticism from across world football. UEFA had warned it could boycott FIFA competitions, including the World Cup, if the plan went ahead.
On Saturday, both UEFA and Concacaf, the governing body for football in North, Central America and the Caribbean, issued statements criticising FIFA's leadership following Infantino's decision to withdraw the proposal.
The FAW is among the first national football associations to publicly oppose Infantino's re-election.
In a statement, the FAW confirmed "its withdrawal of support for the candidature of Gianni Infantino for re-election as Fifa president for the 2027-2031 term".
Explaining its decision, the Welsh governing body said:
"The recent failures in good governance, processes, leadership, values, stakeholder management, communications and sound judgement have led us to a position where Mr Infantino has lost the confidence of the FAW to remain at the helm of world football.
"Failing to put the best interests of football first is a failure we cannot accept."
